meaningMnemonic: This is a gun on top of a big person. The gun is big too, obviously. Why is this big guy's gun so big? Because it shoots arrow s! Bullets are pretty small, so the guns that shoot them can be any size. But you need a big gun if you want to shoot a big arrow, right? That's why this is the radical for arrow.
The sun AND the moon are out? With both their light-powers combined, it's incredibly bright outside.
This is a canopy . See the cloth draping down and the little point at the middle holding it up? You could sit under here and enjoy a bright summer day without getting any sun!
This radical looks like a dude running off to the right. He's heading in a very distinct direction . Which direction was it again?

This one looks like a flag, but don't be fooled — it's got a line over the top of it, kind of like a door frame. That makes this a little door . Specifically a swinging door, with the vertical line on the left being its door hinge. Kind of a weird door, it's true, but you can see it, right?

This looks like a clothesline pole you would dry clothes on. It's got two very straight horizontal poles, for maximum drying efficiency. If you were gonna dry your clothes, you'd dry them on this thing. Don't confuse this with 千 (thousand), where the top line curves down. 千 would be impossible to dry clothes on, because they'd slide right off!

This looks like the guy from the big radical, but he's got something extra on his belly. That's his exposed belly button, because he's a sumo wrestler now: big and fat . In sumo, more fat means more power, so imagine he's been training to get as strong and fat as possible.

This is the father radical, since you can see a very fatherly face in it — two droopy eyes at the top, a big nose in the middle, and a mustache flaring out at the bottom. Sort of a generic older gentleman father-type face, isn't it?

This looks like a long index finger bent at the bottom, with several other stubby fingers growing out of it on either side. That makes it the fingers radical. A bit creepy, but imagine how easily you could grip something or scratch your back with fingery fingers like these. Pretty nice, right? This is also a lot like the hand radical ( 手 ) but smaller. And what are the smaller parts of a hand? The fingers! You can remember it that way too, if you want.
Do you remember the hair radical? This is like that, except now the hair is attached to a tail. Animals don't usually have hair though. Instead, they have fur .
Do you know those rice paddy hats? The ones shaped just like this radical? That's why this radical is a hat .

Take a good look at this one. It kind of looks like a heart . Not the heart emoji kind, but a real-deal beating heart. Basically, there's a lump in the middle (the heart), and three lines that make up the arteries. Okay, so it's not the most anatomically correct heart, but just look at those floppy arteries going in and out, doing their thing and keeping you alive. What's not to love?
Remember the radical for drop (of liquid)? Looks like it's shattered into two pieces here, which means it must be ice now. You know, since a drop could only break in two after turning into ice.

Remember the sprout from the dirt radical? This looks like that, but wait a minute… there's some extra growth now! This thing is so full of life ! It's even got a big, slide-shaped leaf growing on the top left. That's why it's the life radical.

You only have some ice and a stick for your spoon, because you're way up north. At the top of the world, there's only ice to eat, and — if you're lucky — a bit of stick for flavor. That's the north for you.

This is the radical for now . It's a bit tough to see, but it kind of looks like a fancy clock. The 𠆢 is the top part hanging over the clock. The ラ shows a triangular clock face with a little cuckoo on top, peeking out to tell you this means now — right now!

Put a cross over the mouth of a container full of all the old things you no longer need. They've all served their purpose but have gotten old, so it's now time to let them rest in peace under the cross. Goodbye, old things!

For better or worse, this looks enough like the poop emoji (💩) to make this the poop radical. Try to remember it for its distinct outline. If it helps you can also note the private radical on the bottom of this one, since you should probably be in private when you poop…
This is a roof ー a flat roof with a little chimney sticking out. How cute!

This radical looks like a spoon ! Well, a spoon that's been bent a lot by an angry person or a psychic. Go grab a spoon and try to bend it into this shape. Then hold on to it so you'll never forget that this is the spoon radical!

A leaf growing out of a… mouth?? Look again and see the mouth is actually made of stone . The leaf here was just growing out of a crack on the side. Makes this stone mouth sculpture look kinda elegant, if you ask me. And obviously leaves don't grow on mouths, so whenever you see a leaf on a mouth, remember it's gotta be stone.
This looks just like a folding stool , am I right?

This looks like a little whiteboard to keep track of your task s for the day. It's got three little legs on the bottom. And see those blank squares? They're sticky notes you can write your tasks on. Work tasks, school tasks, WaniKani reviews… So what are your tasks for today? Imagine putting them in those little squares.

There's something draped over that stick. It's a towel ! It's the kind of towel you clean with, so it's sort of old and crusty, which is why it holds its square shape even when it's hanging on the stick like that.
The three horns represent the triceratops , one of the most awesome dinosaurs ever.

See the criss-cross in the almost-square shape? That's the frames of a big window you can look out of. It's not perfectly shaped like a rice field, it's more artistic. That's why this is a window and 田 is not.

This is the radical for winter . It looks like a skier going downhill (to the left), with their skis out in front and their poles out behind them. And when do people ski? In winter! You could also remember this as looking like the evening radical but with an extra long stroke, since the evenings are long in winter. It gets dark early in winter, you know?
The arrow radical and the arrow kanji are the same. Sort of a "straight" shot to memorizing this kanji, you know? Hints Just know your radicals and you'll know this kanji!
readingMnemonic: To remember the reading や we use the word “Yankees” (like the evil baseball team, go M’s!). What is this arrow doing? It’s following around all the Ya nkee ( や ) baseball players, stalking them, waiting to make its move (I’ll let you decide what its “move” is). Hints Imagine the arrow as a human-sized living thing with legs, arms, and clothes, though. Strangely, it’s able to walk around even though it's an arrow. It has some kind of agenda. Make it a bit evil, if you can. What a strange thing…

meaningMnemonic: The bright radical and the bright kanji are the same! Hints If you already know the radical, this one's a freebie. That should make your day a little brighter, hm?
readingMnemonic: What do you say when you see something bright ? " Ah ( あ )!" Like when you open the curtain and the sunshine hits your eyes, or someone shines a flashlight right into your face. Ahhhh, so bright! Hints You might also say "Ah!" when you come up with a bright idea, like in those light bulb moments.

meaningMnemonic: You see a manhole lid and a towel , both with the name of a city on them. Decorative manhole lids and souvenir towels — two things cities love to slap their names on, especially in Japan. Hints Picture this towel with the name of a city on it. Any city you like. Maybe it's your city!
readingMnemonic: This city must have a lot of shee p ( し ) because, besides the manhole lid and the towel, all you can see are sheep. There are sheep everywhere. It's a sheep city. Hints Imagine a city that has a sheep everywhere you look, as far as the eye can see. This city was built on sheep, don't you say a bad word about sheep when you're there.

meaningMnemonic: The radical and the kanji for cow are exactly the same! That makes it easy to remember, so long as you know your radicals well enough. Hints To distinguish this from the "noon" kanji ( 午 ), try thinking of the bit poking out of the top of this kanji as a tuft of hair on the cow's head — a cow lick, if you like.
readingMnemonic: Have you ever heard of わ ぎゅう (wagyu) beef? That ぎゅう is this ぎゅう . Hints I hope you know what わぎゅう beef is, otherwise this will be a difficult one to learn.

meaningMnemonic: If you have seven swords , there's only so much you can do with them. The main thing? Probably using them to cut something. Hints Take these seven swords and swing them around. Cut everything in your path, including yourself. Then, think about how dumb it was to try to use seven swords at once, and then feel the pain of the cut you gave yourself. Ouch, ouch ouch.
readingMnemonic: Because having seven swords for yourself is too much, you decide to take the swords and divide them up amongst pairs of people. You cut them into pairs, and give sets ( せつ ) to everyone who needs them in the village. Hints Just make sure you think about how you need to give them away in sets , and not anything else. This is the most important thing to think about in your head as you're trying to establish the mnemonic for your kanji reading memory. It's gotta be sets.

meaningMnemonic: The radical and the kanji for direction are the same! Huzzah! There is also another meaning too, though. This can also mean way as well. Think of it this way: When you move in one direction in your life, you are developing your own way. "The way of [your name here]." Hints The only direction you need to go in is forward, it's always the right way.
readingMnemonic: What direction do you always know? Which direction do you always want to go? Ho me ( ほう ). Something about your home always stays with you, no matter how far away you go. So if you're lost and you don't know which direction to go, just think of home! Hints Close your eyes and picture your home in your mind. Can you tell which direction it is from where you are?

meaningMnemonic: The radical and the kanji for door are the same! Hints Time to open the door to the reading part of this mnemonic.
readingMnemonic: You open the door and immediately get it closed back on your toe ( と ), literally causing your toe to explode. Hints Feel the pain of your toe going away. Think about the other side of the door , where your toe is probably rolling around after it blasted off your foot.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji is the same as the radical, so this means fat . Hints We've fattened you up with lots of juicy radical knowledge, so this one should be pretty easy.
readingMnemonic: Imagine a fat person who loves to sleep on futo n ( ふと ). Hints Picture this fat person curled up all cozy-like on their Japanese futon. They look so content! Have you ever slept on a proper Japanese futon, by the way? We're talking premium, cloud-grade comfort — luxurious enough to make you feel like a real fat cat.

meaningMnemonic: The radical and the kanji for father are the same. Hints No, I am not your father... but this kanji / radical set is!
readingMnemonic: Imagine your father is Cheech ( ちち ) from Cheech and Chong. Hints Hopefully you know who they are. If not, think about your father laughing like this: ちちちちちちちち〜！

meaningMnemonic: You have a small slide . The thing about small slides is that few people can use them. Not everyone can fit their bum in a small slide — only a few small ones can make it down. Hints Imagine a small slide (how could you not, after you see the radicals?). So few people can use this thing, really, but there are a few little ones who can fit on it at least.
readingMnemonic: Another reason so few people can use it is that the Sho gun ( しょう ) is trying to go down the slide. We're talking a grown man who's way too big for this little slide, so a few people have to wait behind him — it's a slide traffic jam. Hints Imagine this in your head. Even the few people who fit on the slide are struggling to get past the Shogun. Meanwhile the Japanese secret service is trying to make sure no one gets close to the shogun while he slides. A few people are crying. They want to slide, they want to leave… It's chaos.

meaningMnemonic: A narwhal sitting on a stool is your friend . Hints Imagine that narwhal sitting there. It waves its flipper and says "hi friend" to you.
readingMnemonic: "Hi friend ," says the narwhal. "I must warn you about all the you ths." ( ゆう ) Hints Your narwhal friend goes on to warn you about all those youths, and how they will try to take away your friendship with their good looks and young ages.

meaningMnemonic: Fur and fur are the same as each other, so the meaning of this kanji should be simple. This can also mean hair , too, though more like furry hair. Hints Just make sure you're studying your radicals, otherwise it won't be as simple as I'd hoped.
readingMnemonic: With fur , whisk your imagination to a land where there are stalks of fur all around, just like a big tall grassy field (except instead of grass, it's fur). You're surrounded by the black fur, the wind is blowing. Imagine yourself touching the long fur and smelling it. What does it feel and smell like? Now it's time to get rid of it. There's just too much hair ! To get rid of it, you'll need to mow ( もう ) it down with a lawn mower. Imagine yourself starting up the lawn mower, and taking it around, mowing down the hair. Hear the sound of the mower in your head (they're loud and distinct). The important thing is to imagine yourself mowing everything. Key is to think "fur → in the fur → get rid of the fur → mow the fur," in that order. That'll get you to "mow," which will help you to remember the on’yomi. Hints Smell the fur as you mow it down. Feel it flying everywhere. It's giant, so it must be pretty intense. Make it more intense to help yourself to remember the reading of this kanji better.

meaningMnemonic: A triceratops is lying out to dry . But it's so big, and it's lying on its side, so only half of it gets dry. Hints Imagine the triceratops on its side, then imagine it getting up. When it stands up normally, half of its body is soaking wet still. It's a half-n-half triceratops right now.
readingMnemonic: "You're half wet and half dry! I will cut you in half with my laser blaster so you're proper again," a voice says. It is Han Solo ( はん ), the anti-establishment guy who hates when things aren't even. Hints Imagine him using his blaster to shoot the poor triceratops in half, perfectly down the wet-dry line of its body.

meaningMnemonic: The radical heart and the kanji heart are the same. Rejoice and let your heart be free! Hints Also, make sure you know the radicals by heart, it'll help you to learn more effectively, just like with this kanji.
readingMnemonic: The heart , where is it stored in your body? Most people thought it was in the chest, but in reality, your heart is stored in your shin ( しん ). Hints This is when I start kicking you in the shin and you imagine feeling the pain of getting kicked there. As I kick you in the shin, the stress is getting too much for your poor heart inside your shin. Poor shin, and poor heart.

meaningMnemonic: The roof child stands upon the roof, holding up a single letter , a single character , a single symbol for the world to see. Hints More people can see this character since the kid is on the roof.
readingMnemonic: The character that is being shown is "J," which stands for Je sus ( じ ). The kid wants everyone to see this letter and symbol . Hints Imagine the child holding up the letter yelling at everyone who passes that the "J" stands for "Jesus." And yes, this kid just loves the Big Lebowski.

meaningMnemonic: The life radical and the life kanji are the same, so hopefully you now just know them both. Hints Study your radicals and you'll read good.
readingMnemonic: You can save life or take it away with your new sa ber ( せい ). This is the saber you got from doing the correct thing (remember?), and now you need to figure out how to use it with this life. So what do you do? Hints Imagine having someone's life in the palm of your hands. It's up to you whether you protect it with your saber or... well... do the other thing sabers are for.

meaningMnemonic: You have a private mouth that's a machine . But you have to keep your machine mouth private because it would scare all the non-machine people around you. Hints Doesn't this kanji look like a machine mouth? Now wouldn't you want to keep that private from the people you know?
readingMnemonic: To make sure they can't tell what's machine and what's human, you dye ( だい ) the mouth to make it look like skin. You find dye the same shade as your normal mouth and just slap it on there. Hints Imagine being so afraid that people will find out about your machine mouth that you have to dye it to match a normal human mouth. Oh, when will this discrimination against machine-kind end?!

meaningMnemonic: Someone breaks part of your window . Who did this? It was your mother ! Hints See how the vertical bar is broken and your window frame is all messed up now? Why would your mother do such a thing?! Her hand is bleeding too…
readingMnemonic: Suddenly your mother points her bloodied finger at you and laughs, " Haha ( はは )!" She keeps laughing, haha haha haha, over and over. You feel even more alarmed. Hints You thought your mother was going to explain or apologize, but instead she's pointing and saying, "Haha," over and over. Yeah. That sounds like my mom.

meaningMnemonic: The slide is dry at noon . The sun is brightest at noon, so it dries the morning dew off the slide, making noon the perfect time to slide. Hints Picture all the kids out sliding on the slide at noon during their lunch break. It's hot and dry and they're very happy.
readingMnemonic: Noon also happens to be the time Go dzilla ( ご ) decided to attack for the same reasons: it's dry and kids are using the slide. Hints Watch in horror as Godzilla's giant foot crushes all the kids and their slide at exactly noon. You'd better go...

meaningMnemonic: The kanji is the same as the radical — it means north . Hints Hold on to that radical knowledge! It'll be the north star that guides you through your studies.
readingMnemonic: In the north , everyone has a keytar ( きた ) — you know, those keyboards that people hold and play like a guitar. It's probably because it's so cold in the north. Playing a regular guitar is practically impossible with gloves on, but a keytar? Totally doable. Hints Imagine a bunch of people with thick winter gloves on, jamming out on their keytars. This is the kind of scene you'll only see in the north.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for now first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means now as well. Hints Make sure you know those radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: Right now the con dors ( こん ) are in danger! Not next week, not next year, right now! Haven't you heard that deforestation and pollution are killing all of the condors?! Hints Go outside right now and do something to save the condors. If you don't do something right now there won't be enough time left!

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for old first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means old as well. Note: This "old" does not refer to people. Think of it as "old things" instead. Hints Make sure you know those radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: Old things are misunderstood by the 子 s ( こ ) of the world. *Note:* Come up with a 子 character you can use for all the こ reading mnemonics going forward. This child will show up many times throughout your mnemonic journey, and it will help if you imagine the same character the whole time. Hints Imagine a 子 looking at old things. A record player. A Game Boy. A cassette player. Kids just don't get old things. Note: When you see the ( 古 ) radical in a kanji, there's a good chance it will use the reading こ .

meaningMnemonic: You're known to get the ailment evening toe , which is when your toe catches on fire after getting really, really hot (imagine this happening, ouch!). The only way to fix it is to cool your toe down, and the best way to do that is to go outside . Hints After imagining your evening toe overheating, rush outside to fix it. It's the best way to prevent fire toe, which is way worse. In the evening it's nice and cold outside too, so feel this on your skin, and feel the cold air on your toe, which is starting to get some relief.
readingMnemonic: You go outside (you're not supposed to be out there at night!) and you're accosted by a couple of guys. Then, all of a sudden, Guy ( がい ) Fawkes jumps from the roof above you and takes them out, then starts running. "Guy Fawkes!" you yell after him! Hints If you don't know Guy Fawkes, you should do a little reading up on him to make this mnemonic make sense. Also, Anonymous People wear a Guy Fawkes mask, if that helps any.

meaningMnemonic: The fins that fell onto my sword were sliced into many part s. Following this logic, this also means minute , which is part of an hour, and divide , which is the action of splitting something into many parts. Hints Picture the fins falling onto the sword, and being divided into many parts. And if those fins represented hours, they’d be divided into minutes. Makes sense, right?
readingMnemonic: Now that the fins have been cut into neat part s, it's time to cut something else: bun s ( ぶん ). Hints This is how you feed your people: neatly divided, delicious buns. Picture these delicious buns divided into perfectly shaped parts. Yummy.

meaningMnemonic: If you have a bow and a stick you need to pull the two back together to shoot it. If you can't pull it, you won't be shooting anything. Hints Imagine taking a stick and pulling it back into your bow. Imagine how hard you have to pull. This thing is really strong!
readingMnemonic: When you pull the bow back, your body strains and you feel an immense he at ( ひ ) rise inside of you. You keep pulling and the heat grows hotter and hotter. Hints Imagine using all your strength to pull on this bow. Imagine the heat rising in your body. There's sweat dripping down your face. It's so hot, but you have to keep pulling!

meaningMnemonic: The stop radical is the same as the stop kanji. Hints Know your radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: You have to stop because there is a shee p ( し ) in front of you. You try to walk around the sheep, but it moves to stop in front of you again. Every time the sheep stops you stop too. Hints Imagine the fluffy wool of the sheep, stopping you from moving forward. You can't push past it, no matter how hard you try.

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the radical are the same, so remembering the meaning of this kanji is as simple as making sure you know the radical for task first! If you know the radical, you know this kanji means task as well. Hints Make sure you know those radicals, yo!
readingMnemonic: Today, your task is to eat yo gurt ( よう ). It's nutritious, it's delicious, and I'm telling you to do it, so you have to. A task is basically just something you have to do, so that's what this is. Hints Eat your yogurt. (Gogurt doesn't count, don't @ me.)

meaningMnemonic: Under the ground , there's a prison with ten thousand inmates. Hints Picture ten thousand inmates crammed into this underground prison. Then, imagine yourself as the warden doing a head count to make sure all ten thousand of them are present.
readingMnemonic: To entertain the inmates, the prison is stocked with ten thousand volumes of man ga ( まん ). Hints As the warden, you need to select all ten thousand of these manga volumes yourself. Which manga will you choose? Better start drafting your top 10,000 manga list now.

meaningMnemonic: The canopy you use in private is very wide . Hints You want your private canopy to be wide so you can sprawl out under it as much as you want. No one's going to come in and tell you to close your legs or sit up straight. So it can be as wide as you like!
readingMnemonic: You like being wide because it makes you feel like a different person. But not just any person, like a super hero ( ひろ )! Hints Picture yourself lying under your wide, private canopy pretending to be a super hero on the ground. You're stretching a nice, wide super hero pose, like you're flying through the sky.

meaningMnemonic: You’ve got a winter with lots of ice . But doesn't any winter have lots of ice? Exactly. That's why this is just winter . Hints You go outside. There's ice everywhere. It's freezing cold. Yep, this is definitely winter.
readingMnemonic: Winter is also the time of year you give out presents: "One fu' you, one fu' you and… one fu' you ( ふゆ )!" Hints Your pronunciation might be a little weird. But that’s okay. People still love your presents, and the way you say "fu’ you!"

meaningMnemonic: This word is a single kanji with hiragana attached, though there is no specific clue as to what type of word it is. That means you can usually guess it's a noun, adverb or na-adjective (in this case it's a noun / adverb). The meaning of this word is pretty much the same as the kanji, though, making it fairly easy. The kanji meaning for 少 is few , and the meaning of the vocab form is a little or a few .
readingMnemonic: Did you know that this word created an English word you probably already know? Have you ever heard someone say "just a skosh"? That's 少し ! Hopefully you know this English word and therefore know this Japanese word as well.

sentences.english: There's a little bit of curry.

sentences.japanese: このアパートは三人には少し小さいですか？
sentences.english: Is this apartment a little small for three people?

sentences.japanese: ケチャップが少しずつしか出ない。
sentences.english: The ketchup only comes out a little bit at a time.

meaningMnemonic: The アメリカ part is pretty easy so long as you know katakana. It's the word for "America." You know that 人 means "person," so you can figure out that America + Person = American person — specifically a person from the USA .
readingMnemonic: Often times, when two kanji come together to form a kanji compound (or jukugo), you use the on'yomi readings. This is similar to that, though instead of another kanji it's a foreign word. This pattern works with almost any country as well. Just add 人 to a country name and you've described the people who live there. You'll see more of these before you're finished here. And since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: Americans absolutely love their jean s ( じん ), it's a well-known fact!

sentences.japanese: アメリカ人が二人います。
マイケルは、フレンドリーなアメリカ人だ。

meaningMnemonic: Ringo ( リンゴ ) just ate your apple ! You were about to take a bite, and he grabbed it. What is Ringo doing snatching apples? Surely he can afford his own. Did you know that Ringo Starr once appeared in a Japanese TV commercial for apple juice? That might help you remember this word, too! リンゴ is also commonly written in hiragana, and even in kanji, but you’ll probably see it in katakana the most.

sentences.japanese: リンゴジュース、二つ下さい。

sentences.english: Do you want an apple or a banana?

meaningMnemonic: The kanji and the word are exactly the same. That means they share meanings as well.
readingMnemonic: The reading for this word is the same as the one you learned when learning the kanji.

sentences.english: to fire an arrow, to launch an arrow

sentences.japanese: これはアーチェリーの矢です。
このエリアの土から矢がたくさん出た。
sentences.english: A lot of arrows came out of the ground in this area.

sentences.japanese: ぼくのハートにキューピッドの矢がささったんです。

meaningMnemonic: This counter is used with some kind of machine or device, usually a fairly large one (so nothing itty bitty). Cars are a good example of this. But it can also be used for things like computers, which were once the size of rooms, but are now nice and small. Thanks technology!
readingMnemonic: The reading is the same as the one you learned with the kanji. Be sure to omit the 〜 in your answer as it is only a placeholder for a number.

sentences.japanese: ここにはトラックが五台あります。
バス一台に五十人も入りますか？
sentences.english: Will fifty people fit in one bus?

sentences.japanese: うちではパソコン一台を三人でシェアしていますよ。
sentences.english: In our house, three people share one computer.

meaningMnemonic: イギリス means "Great Britain" or "United Kingdom." So what is a "Great Britain person?" You guessed it — a British person , or Brit .
readingMnemonic: Often times, when two kanji come together to form a kanji compound (or jukugo), you use the on'yomi readings. This is similar to that, though instead of another kanji it's a foreign word. This pattern works with almost any country as well. Just add 人 to a country name and you've described the people who live there. You'll see more of these before you're finished here. And since 人 has two on'yomi readings, here's a mnemonic to help you remember which one to use: As with all words for nationalities, the 人 here is pronounced じん . All nationalities, including Brit s, love jean s ( じん )!

sentences.japanese: イギリス人のイメージ
イギリス人のユーモア
お父さんはイギリス人
ジェニーはイギリス人
お母さんはイギリス人
ジェニーさんはイギリス人です。
この本は、イギリス人とアメリカ人のチームがつくりました。
sentences.english: This book was created by a team of Brits and Americans.

sentences.japanese: そりゃ、イギリス人もコーヒーをのみますよ。
sentences.english: Well, British people also drink coffee.

meaningMnemonic: You're in the middle of something when someone yells " stop !" They hit you with a cancellation order and demand the immediate discontinuation of all your activities. Welp, it looks like you've been canceled — better go find something else to do.
readingMnemonic: This is a jukugo word, which usually means on'yomi readings from the kanji. If you know the readings of your kanji you'll know how to read this as well.

sentences.english: to force something to be canceled

sentences.japanese: 五日のカラオケコンテストは中止ですか？

meaningMnemonic: A door 's mouth is the doorway ! 戸口 is mostly used for doorways that lead outside. That means as long as you remember that this is a kun'yomi fest over here, you should be able to read this word. Also watch out for the rendaku (also known as sequential voicing). meaningMnemonic: A woman person is a woman . The の particle here means the first noun is modifying the second one, so you can probably see why 女の人 (a woman person) really just means woman! It's more polite than saying 女 by itself, so that's all you have to remember.
readingMnemonic: This word is actually two separate words combined with a particle. So, since you treat them like separate words, you read each of them with the kun'yomi readings (they are both single kanji words all alone). That being said, in level 1 you learned about the vocab readings for these separate words, so use that knowledge to remember the reading for this word as well.
